newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY COALITION NOT FULLY IN ACCORD AFTER SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY COALITION NOT FULLY IN ACCORD AFTER SCANDAL.

text.p: The junior party in Hungary's ruling coalition withheld full backing on Wednesday for appointees to replace Industry and Trade Minister Tamas Suchman, sacked over a scandal at the privatisation agency.

The government also said it would investigate the scandal "in the most minute detail" to determine how a consultant was illegally awarded a contract from privatisation agency APV Rt which paid her more than 800 million forints ($5.2 million).

After a fence-mending meeting of the coalition, the junior partner Free Democrats (SZDSZ) endorsed Socialist Prime Minister's Gyula Horn's nomination for industry and trade minister but stopped short of publicly backing his choice for the privatisation portfolio.
Horn has named Szabolcs Fazakas as industry and trade minister and Judit Csiha as privatisation minister to replace Suchman who held both posts until he was sacked last week.
"The position that we support the nomination of Szabolcs Fazakas is public," Free Democrat MP Tamas Bauer told Reuters. "We will make our position on Judit Csiha clear in a few days."
Fazakas, seen as a technocrat, was state secretary at the industry and trade ministry until the summer when he was named ambassador to Germany, Hungary's biggest trade partner.
Csiha, a lawyer who is state secretary at the justice ministry, is seen as a more political appointee. She was once head of the Socialist Party faction in Budapest's City Council.
Both need the support of the Free Democrats in order to gain the parliamentary approval needed for their appointments.
At a briefing for foreign journalists, government spokesman Elemer Kiss said the government was speeding up its investigation of the scandal and would not allow it to drag on.
"It is the position of the government...that this case has to be investigated in the most minute detail and action taken concerning those who should be held responsible," Kiss said.
He added that while the scandal involved APV officials, "the matter has no direct linkage to privatisation itself".
"This matter should not affect or in any major way delay the privatisation practices of the government," he said.
Kiss said the government had already begun security checks for nine potential new members of the APV board of directors and said they should be appointed within a matter of a week.
He said the government had acted immediately once it was advised that the APV's contract with the consultant, Marta Tocsik, was illegal, by sacking APV directors and Suchman.

"This, if you like, is a message to all those working or active in the economic sphere that in your activity you have to consider and bear in mind when you vote and when you sign something," Kiss said.
